Subject: Sizing and hosting posture for regulated inference — TheraHealth pilot

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks for the quick intro last week. We're scoping a 3-month pilot for TheraHealth to run Protected Health Information (PHI) workflows for our clinical summarization and triage features. Before we schedule an architecture session, can you confirm whether Redwood can provide:

- A head-to-head comparison of Dedicated (reserved) vs Private (VPC/on-prem) footprints for a regulated pilot (cost, latency, failover, operational overhead)
- Suggested GPU counts and autoscale bands for the expected load (see below)
- Any constraints around SOC 2 / data residency and how they change the sizing or runbook

Workload profile (initial pilot):
- Average QPS: 35 requests/s; peak burst expected to 220 requests/s for short windows
- Average prompt length: 600 input tokens, expected output ~350 tokens
- Expected daily token volume (pilot): ~1.3M tokens
- 99p latency objective: <= 350ms for single-turn generation
- Data retention: logs kept for 90 days, with encrypted-at-rest requirements; some customers require dedicated tenancy

Attached: TheraHealth_Requirements_v1.pdf (list of compliance asks + sample transcripts).

Primary asks: a) rough Dedicated vs Private sizing and delta in cost/ops; b) recommended pilot hosting posture to unblock procurement.

Thanks — happy to loop in our procurement contact (procure@therahealth.ai) and an external cloud partner (Glen Klein) if helpful.

—Leah
Leah Moss
Head of Product
TheraHealth

Leah — thanks for the clear summary and the attachment. Short answer: yes, we can run the pilot in either Dedicated (reserved GPU pool) or Private (VPC/on-prem) modes; the tradeoffs are mostly about headroom for burst, operator effort, and peripheral costs (networking, on-prem ops, audit evidence cadence).

Quick proposal for next steps:
1) I’ll ask Karthik to draft a two-column sizing snapshot (Dedicated vs Private) with recommended min/nominal/max GPU counts and an autoscaling band for the pilot profile.
2) Marissa will surface commercial paths (pilot pricing, commitment tiers, MSA redline considerations).
3) If you can share an expected procurement timeline, we’ll align the mutual action plan.

Operational notes up front:
- For peaks to 220 rps we recommend enabling prefix/KV caching where feasible — that reduces effective GPU load by up to ~25% for repeated prompt shapes.
- Quantized model variants (4-bit) are usually a good trade for throughput if you can tolerate a small quality delta; we’ll include quality/regression guardrails.

Looping Karthik and Marissa in for the sizing + commercial detail.

Cheers,
Kimberly Park
Director, Deal Engineering | Redwood Inference
From: karthik_iyer@redwood.com

Leah / Team — moved the math here after reviewing the profile and sample transcripts. High-level assumptions: 2.0 tokens/s per generated token (model + infra overhead), average total tokens per request ~950, peak concurrency windows ~220 rps for up to 90s, production SLO 99p <= 350ms.

Sizing snapshot (pilot — single region):
1) Dedicated (Redwood reserved pool, multi-tenant but isolated pool):
   - Baseline (min/keepwarm): 3 x A100-80GB-equivalent GPUs (handles steady 35 rps with headroom, prefix cache enabled)
   - Nominal (target throughput): 10 x A100 (covers typical peak + burst smoothing with autoscaling to handle 220 rps bursts via warm pooling)
   - Max (burst capacity with aggressive autoscale): up to 18 x A100 (for sustained high windows; enables graceful degradation policies)
   - Autoscale policy suggestion: min=3, target_concurrency_per_gpu=22-28, max=18; burst buffer of warm spare GPUs to avoid cold-start latency.

2) Private (VPC-managed or on-prem isolated fleet):
   - Baseline (min/keepwarm): 6 x A100 (higher baseline for redundancy & HA in private setups)
   - Nominal: 14 x A100 (higher than Dedicated because operator overhead and on-prem provisioning reduces elastic bursting to the public pool)
   - Max: recommend planning for 22 x A100 (to cover failover, replication, and maintenance windows without impacting pilot)
   - Autoscale policy suggestion: min=6, max=22; plan for scheduled buffer for backup nodes and capacity held for snapshots/replication.

Why Private needs more GPUs: redundancy (+N), air-gap or limited network egress, and limited ability to burst into shared cloud capacity. Private often needs extra headroom for in-place failover and batched maintenance.

Performance levers and cost controls:
- KV/prefix caching: up to ~20–30% effective request reduction for repeated templates.
- Quantization: 4-bit variants give ~1.8–2x throughput improvements; we recommend running a short eval to measure quality delta on clinical summaries.
- Dynamic routing: route low-latency/critical requests to Dedicated and archival/non-urgent to Private to optimize unit cost.

Estimated infra delta (very rough):
- Dedicated nominal (10 GPUs): baseline infra cost X
- Private nominal (14 GPUs): ~+35–45% infra op cost (includes on-call, patching, replication) — we’ll produce a detailed cost model per your procurement ask.

Attached: gpu-forecast-v2.xlsx (workbook with token-level math and cost estimators).

Happy to walkthrough the workbook in a 30m call.

—Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Principal Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

High-level commercial path we propose:
- 3-month pilot on Dedicated: reduced pilot rate, limited committed GPUs (we can commit to nominal = 10 GPUs with burst pricing up to 18)
- Optional conversion to Private: transition window agreed in MAP, procurement files (MSA + SOC2 addendum) to be completed during month 2

Action items for TheraHealth to unblock pricing and procurement:
1) confirm procurement timeline and PO owner (procure@therahealth.ai seems right)
2) confirm whether encryption key management must be customer-managed (KMS/HSM)
3) sign mutual_action_plan.docx so we can lock the pilot commercial terms and start provisioning.

I’ll send a draft MAP and an initial SOW/quote once we have PO and KMS info.

Cheers,
Marissa Cole
